title: Up the cliffs of Difensa

facts.text: The First Special Service Force was a single unit of American and Canadian volunteers under one chain of command, activated in July 1942 and trained in Montana for winter raids in Norway that never happened.

By late 1943 the Fifth Army was stuck at the German Winter Line south of Cassino. Monte la Difensa, Hill 960, looked down on the road to Rome, and an American regiment had already failed to take it in November.
At 4.30 p.m. on 2 December 1943 the guns opened up. Of 925 artillery pieces firing in Operation Raincoat, 346 aimed at Difensa alone and fired more than 22,000 rounds in an hour.
At dusk the Force's 2nd Regiment, about 600 men, started up the steep northern face for a surprise attack, through rain, fog and snow. The Force's commander was Col. Robert T. Frederick, 36.
The last 500 feet were sheer cliff. Scouts Sgt. Thomas Fenton and Sgt. Howard Van Ausdale climbed ahead and anchored ropes, and the men hauled themselves up in the dark with their weapons.

Some men slipped on loose gravel and the Germans fired flares. The Forcemen reached the crest shortly before dawn on 3 December and cleared the summit in about two hours. Fifth Army planners had expected it to take two or three days.
The cost was heavy. Lt. Col. Thomas MacWilliam, commanding the regiment's 1st Battalion, was killed, as was Capt. William Rothlin, one of his company commanders.
Then came three days of rain, sleet and freezing cold on the bare summit, with every load of food and ammunition carried up by hand. On 4 December Frederick signalled: "Every man in unit exhausted."
In six days the Force lost 511 men: 73 dead, 9 missing, 313 wounded or injured and 116 evacuated for exposure and exhaustion. The 142nd Infantry relieved them on 8 December.
Frederick went on to lead the Force through Anzio and into Rome, and by the end of the war he had earned eight Purple Hearts.

At Anzio, Frederick later said, a dead German officer's diary called them the black devils, who came all around and were never heard. The Forcemen, who blackened their faces for night raids, preferred another name: the Devil's Brigade.

On 5 December 1944, almost a year to the day after Difensa, the Force paraded for the last time as its Canadians left. Its battle honours live on in the Canadian Special Operations Regiment and the U.S. Special Forces.

Men of the 3rd Regiment, First Special Service Force, laden with packs, climb a rocky, muddy mountain track past a mule relay point in the Cervaro area, Italy, winter 1943 to 1944 (the Force fought at Cervaro in January 1944; NARA gives no exact date). Foreground: T/4 Harlan Morgan of Leroy, Montana. Photo by Gallagher, 163rd Signal Photo Company, U.S. Army Signal Corps, NARA 111-SC-218510-1 (NAID 404790740), public domain. Saved 1800 x 1382, cropped from the 2988 x 2399 NARA scan; print number and Signal Corps stamp left in at the edges. Not Difensa itself (no photos of the assault are known); chosen because it shows the same men in the same mountains and weather, faces and loads in motion. Runner up: Brig. Gen. Robert T. Frederick with Maj. Gen. John P. Lucas, Nettuno area, 2 February 1944, NARA 111-SC-212642.

declassified.fact: Pfc. Kenneth Thelen was hit 18 times on the mountain and suffered two broken arms and two broken legs. He lay on the summit for about a day and a half before he could be moved, and carrying him down took another 18 hours.

NOON: 03:18 to 04:56: a U.S. heavy howitzer (240mm type) crew in a sandbagged pit loading and firing (03:28 muzzle blast, 04:20 to 04:56 loading the big shell and firing, smoke at 04:50); open on the muzzle blast at 03:28 or 04:50. 7 P.M. SECOND CUT: 00:10 to 03:10: Force men resting on a rocky mountainside, a soldier with a shoulder patch (00:20), helmeted men studying a map (00:30), soldiers climbing with heavy packs (01:00 to 01:55), a soldier on a skyline ridge (02:30), the mountain valley (02:50 to 03:10); open on the climb at 01:40. 05:00 to 06:10 the same howitzer crew again (unused).
